headline: Sanofi's $41 billion Insmed deal gave healthcare a rare megadeal, while a weeks-long tech and AI selloff, Nvidia's turmoil and the new Anthropic shares dominated markets. Investors now wait on PCE inflation, a second look at Q3 GDP and a fresh round of US tariffs.
watch: October PCE inflation and the second estimate of Q3 GDP, with the Fed's rate path in focus
The US tariff announcement on China and other major economies, and Beijing's response
Whether Anthropic shares recover above the $83 IPO price and what that means for the AI trade and the IPO pipeline
The OPEC+ meeting this weekend and oil's reaction to a possible supply surplus
Follow-up on Sanofi–Insmed and any further large biopharma M&A

paragraphs.text: Sanofi's agreement to buy Insmed for $41 billion in cash is the biggest story. WSJ Health, Endpoints and Fierce Biotech all call it the largest pharma deal of the year, and Endpoints says it is the first biopharma megadeal since Pfizer's $43 billion takeover. Insmed brings Sanofi rare disease and respiratory drugs, including three commercial and late-phase respiratory assets per Fierce. The logic is to offset the coming loss of exclusivity on Dupixent. It is also the first big move by new CEO Belén Garijo. Endpoints reports Sanofi shares rose more than 10% on Tuesday, so investors appear to have welcomed the price and the strategy. A Bloomberg piece says the deal 'looks almost too good', though the headline is all we have and it is not clear what the argument is. A listed fund manager quoted by DirectorsTalk said it benefits from the takeover, a reminder that the deal also lifts the biotech sector's read-through.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere in biotech finance, Endpoints says Kymera priced an upsized $1.75 billion follow-on offering after strong data, the largest follow-on ever for a biotech. Fierce notes Iambic has just completed a $150 million IPO and is already showing preclinical oncology data. Bayer told the WSJ its next pharma deals may target more midstage assets, a shift from its recent focus on early-stage ones. On the corporate side, Bristol Myers is looking internally for a new CFO as David Elkins heads to Coca-Cola, and Orca Bio has made layoffs only months after launching Tregzi.

paragraphs.text: The FDA was busy. BridgeBio won approval for Welgemda in limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9, and analysts quoted by BioPharma Dive see blockbuster potential at a price near $1 million a year. Roche's Wilserdly became the first oral SERD approved in early-stage breast cancer, which Fierce calls the class's biggest commercial test. AbbVie's Rinvoq cleared in vitiligo, setting up competition with Incyte's Opzelura. Cogent's Ekitna, used with Pfizer's Sutent, was approved for second-line GI stromal tumors ahead of its first launch. The agency will also require patient labels to flag accelerated approval, and it cited two drugmakers for failing to report trial results, which STAT calls rare. In medtech, Siemens Healthineers received de novo authorization for an MS blood test and Thermo Fisher won an expanded clearance.

paragraphs.text: Pricing and coverage policy produced several items worth tracking. CMS published negotiated Medicare prices for 13 drugs in the third round, including Lilly's Trulicity and Gilead's Biktarvy, and says they would have saved about $9.2 billion, or 45%, in 2025. Academic hospital leaders are asking Congress for a two-year delay to the 340B reimbursement cut finalized this month, which they say would cost about $5.5 billion. Analysts estimate the proposed Medicare Advantage star-ratings changes could remove more than $100 billion in federal spending over ten years. On the demand side, RWJF finds fewer plan choices on ACA exchanges, WTW expects global health insurance costs to rise 10.2% next year, and a poll finds half of voters paying more this year. The WSJ says Democratic Medicare for All ambitions are already narrowing toward incremental steps.

A WSJ-cited study finds fewer newborns getting the hepatitis B birth dose since a federal panel dropped its longstanding recommendation. Florida's attorney general has sued the Leapfrog Group over its hospital safety grades, following a similar Tenet suit. HHS-related items are also in the news, with RFK Jr.'s redacted calendar published and $47 million awarded to the first MAHA model cohort.

paragraphs.text: The tech selloff is the dominant theme. Bloomberg says the global rout shows no sign of easing as AI doubts accumulate, with investors moving into bonds, and the FT has the Nasdaq 100 set to open lower after weeks of selling. The WSJ ties the fresh weakness to the fading of Monday's rally, which was powered by Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO. Nvidia remains a source of volatility. NYT reports that Justice Department investigators have gathered evidence of its chips being diverted to China by other firms, and lawmakers released data showing Commerce approved sales of more than 800,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. The FT lists the probes from federal and state authorities, Congress and shareholders. Huang apologized to staff and told them he still does not favor succession planning. The list does not explain how his departure and reinstatement came about, so read those items for context.

paragraphs.text: Rates are the other pressure point. Societe Generale told the WSJ that expectations of aggressive Fed tightening are lifting the dollar. Bloomberg says bond traders are hedging a 'hike now, cut later' path in case higher rates tip the economy over. Fed's John Williams said higher rates are likely over time and expects inflation to move closer to 2% in 2027. One strategist, Michael Darda, argues in MarketWatch that markets should welcome a Fed willing to slow demand. Treasury and European yields fell ahead of October PCE and the second Q3 GDP estimate, consistent with a haven bid.

paragraphs.text: Strategists are using the drawdown to argue for the long run. JPMorgan sees the S&P 500 at 8,200 and says the market should move from judging AI by capex to judging adoption. Deutsche Bank's Binky Chadha holds a 9,000 target and expects a 25% rally by the end of next year from the current rout. Not everyone is calm: the WSJ is running a piece on what a bust would do to the US economy, with economists divided on the size of the hit. Consumer confidence offered support, with the Conference Board index at 103.3 versus 91.9 in October and a 92.2 consensus. Home price growth held steady in September, and the WSJ says world trade flows surged on AI-related goods despite more import restrictions.

paragraphs.text: Abroad, central banks are still leaning hawkish. Australian CPI rose 4.9% in October, keeping the RBA ready to hike further even as growth slows. Bank of Canada Governor Macklem expects inflation to stay persistent given Middle East conflict effects. The FT's Monetary Policy Radar sees more ECB tightening, and eurozone capitals are looking for a role for Dutch contender Knot as they back a Spanish candidate to lead the bank. German business sentiment improved again, but UK household energy bills will rise 26% from January on gas costs. ING says a 'full unwind' is underway in emerging-market currencies, citing the tech selloff, narrowing rate premiums and tariff risk.

paragraphs.text: Trade policy is a live risk. The FT and WSJ say new tariffs on China, the EU, Japan and South Korea are expected this week, aimed at excess industrial capacity. China called the prospect political maneuvering and urged both sides to protect the truce. Separately, China extended a suspension of some critical-material export curbs until January and issued a list of demands to Brussels on EU trade talks. Copper is heading for one of its worst months in over a decade on risk aversion and tariff uncertainty, though the WSJ says physical supply stays tight. Oil fell on supply-surplus expectations before this weekend's OPEC+ meeting and renewed Middle East tension.

paragraphs.text: Corporate results were mixed. Dell said its AI-driven sales more than doubled and its backlog is vetted for customer quality, per MarketWatch. Deere's profit fell on weaker large ag equipment sales. EasyJet's profit fell 96% on fuel costs and softer demand in its last annual results before the Apollo takeover. Remy Cointreau rose 11% after lifting guidance, Prosus posted lower net profit on a smaller Tencent sale gain, and Li Auto logged a third straight quarterly loss despite higher sales. Shein's profit rose on lower revenue, and it will pay $100 million to settle US deception allegations.

paragraphs.text: The weakest credit signal comes from AI financing. CNBC says fears about some companies' AI debt rose on Tuesday, a day after Huang's return, which it ties to his role as a kind of banker to the AI boom. The FT's look at the Ellisons' $87 billion debt gamble for Hollywood says it has rattled credit markets and sets up thousands of layoffs, though the blurb does not give terms. The FT also reports that UK pensions regulator chair Emma Douglas is worried schemes may not know their exposure to AI, a theme that matters if AI-linked debt or equity keeps sliding.

paragraphs.text: Corporate stress in Europe is also visible. McKinsey research, reported by the FT and Bloomberg, finds about half of European industrial companies (45% in one account) show financial stress or distress, putting about 3.7 million jobs at risk, with energy and labor costs, weak investment and global competition cited. Meanwhile Aareal Bank is nearing a significible risk transfer on about €2.5 billion of commercial real estate loans for a premium above 12%, only its second such deal. That price shows how much investors demand to take on CRE risk.

paragraphs.text: Private credit is drawing attention on both supply and sentiment. A Seeking Alpha piece on KKR, headlined as a sardonic call for the last private credit fund to turn off the lights, signals skepticism. Fundraising and product launches continue regardless. Ignite has hired from ThinCats to strengthen its lending team, Sundaram Alts is taking an offshore LP for a special situations fund, and ICICI Prudential AMC is seeking $800 million for alternative funds. Truleum Venture Partners launched a tokenized private credit fund, and Pengana Global Private Credit Trust gave a buy-back update. FT Alphaville says BlackRock wants to launch private market ETFs. Details on any of these are thin.

The effect has spread: Nscale's CEO told staff it can stay private as the sell-off threatens its $35 billion IPO, and one outlet says UK law firms benefited from the New York listing.
